text: 普鲁士的军官习惯在地图上计算行军的日程，西里西亚的厂主则计算煤铁运到柏林的价钱。他们都盼望铁路，却未必愿意为同一条线路付钱。把这些腹地连接起来，将使国家拥有比外交辞令更可靠的力量。
匈牙利问题暂时有了结果，各地的争论却没有因此停止。布拉格的学者要求自己的学校，维也纳的官员希望地方能够执行统一的政令。新一轮建设要回答的，是中央政府究竟准备怎样维系这些语言与利益各不相同的省份。
坦志麦特留下了法令，也留下了没有兑现的愿望。沿海商人希望货物能够运出去，内地的官员则抱怨税收不足。国家若要摆脱对外债与战争赔款的忧虑，必须让港口、商路和地方行政真正运转起来。
棉花沿尼罗河运往海岸，外来的布匹又从港口运回内地。军队和政府从这种往来中征税，埃及的工匠却希望得到自己的工场。学校、纺织业与港口能否一同发展，将决定埃及面对周围强国时有多少回旋余地。
首都已经建立自己的权威，命令却常常到不了地方。军人把持的道路、缺少经费的学校和依赖进口工具的工场，都在消耗独立留下的希望。地方需要看得见的建设，政府也需要能够办事的人。
奴隶制的法律已经废除，南方的劳动与土地关系却不会随一纸法令重新安排。获得自由的人需要学校和工作，商人希望恢复交通，旧种植园主则仍在争取地方权力。联邦政府无法只用庆祝自由的演说回答这些问题。
利马的商人面向大海，山区的矿工却首先要面对崎岖的道路。矿石出山的代价决定着工钱与利润，也决定地方有多少税款可用。秘鲁需要连接山地与海岸的交通，更需要能够经营矿场和铁路的人才。
建设与制度条件均已具备
累计#v 12个月#!达到上述条件。
本国拥有的[concept_state]已不足#v 两个#!。
从西里西亚抵达的列车给柏林带来了煤铁，也带来了新的请愿。铁路公司要求支持干线运输，工场主则希望扩大机器和工具的生产。军官们当然赞成增加运力，只是他们给每一座车站都另算了一笔军用的账。政府现在可以决定下一笔支持投向何处。
先让铁路承担更多运输。
工场需要自己的机器与工具。
地方学校已经开始培养新一代教师和办事人员。有人希望他们留在本地，也有人主张将他们纳入维也纳的行政体系。两种意见都声称是在维护国家；真正的分歧，是地方应当得到更多教育资源，还是让中央获得更强的办事能力。
先充实中央的行政机关。
港口的货运和官署的税册开始显示建设的成果。商人请求把支持留在航运事业上，财政官员却认为现在正是整顿行政的机会。政府不能永远靠临时征收解决困难，接下来的投入必须有所取舍。
让税政与行政能够长期维持。
埃及的工场已经能够将更多棉花织成布匹。厂主请求扩大生产，学校的教员则提醒政府：若识字和技艺仍只掌握在少数人手里，新产业很快又会缺少人才。繁荣的开端带来了新的选择。
地方学校、港口和工场的建设，使政府第一次有了比宣言更具体的政绩。各州的代表希望这份支持能够留下来，首都的执政者则主张巩固中央威信。地方工程可以继续扩展，政治上的信用却未必会自动归于政府。
这是政府重新赢得信任的机会。
南方的学校和交通事业已经恢复了一些活力。摆脱奴役的人们要求受教育的机会，商界则催促联邦继续扶助铁路。摆脱奴隶制只是开始；获得自由的人是否能在新的经济秩序中立足，仍取决于今后的投入。
扩大公民受教育的机会。
让南方的交通恢复繁荣。
铁路已经把部分矿区与海岸连接起来，利马的商人开始谈论更大的投资。矿主希望乘势扩张，工程师却担心人才不足会让新的设备闲置。政府可以扶助矿业继续生产，也可以把这一阶段的成果用于培养矿务与工程人才。
我们需要能够掌握这些技术的人。
局势已经改变，这项安排无法实行。
当初提出的建设议程未能如愿完成。办学、工场与交通仍是国家必须面对的问题，但围绕这一轮计划形成的政治期待已经散去。留下的建筑属于今后的生活，未兑现的承诺也会被人记住。

Prussian officers calculate marching times; Silesian manufacturers calculate the cost of sending coal and iron to Berlin. Both want railways, though they may disagree over which lines deserve support. Connecting these regions would give the country a firmer foundation than diplomatic promises alone.

The Hungarian question has reached a settlement, but debate across the country continues. Scholars in Prague seek support for their schools, while officials in Vienna want provincial administrations capable of carrying out common policies. New investment will help determine how the central government holds together provinces with different languages and interests.

The Tanzimat has left laws and unfulfilled ambitions. Coastal merchants want to move their goods; provincial officials complain of inadequate revenues. If the country is to escape its dependence on debt and the costs of war, its ports and administration must sustain more than promises of reform.

Cotton travels down the Nile to the coast, while imported cloth makes the return journey. The army and government tax this commerce, but Egyptian craftsmen want workshops of their own. The development of schools, textiles and ports will shape Egypt's room for manoeuvre among its neighbours and foreign powers.

The capital has established its authority, yet its decisions often fail to reach the provinces. Roads controlled by military strongmen, schools without funds and workshops dependent on imported tools consume the hopes left by independence. The provinces need visible improvements, and the government needs people who can carry them through.

Slavery has been abolished in law, but labour and landholding in the South will not be transformed by proclamation alone. Freed people need schools and work. Merchants want transport restored, while former slaveholders seek to preserve local power. Celebrations of freedom cannot settle these questions.

Lima's merchants look out to sea, while miners in the interior must first contend with mountain roads. The cost of bringing ore to market shapes wages, profits and provincial revenues. Peru needs connections between its mines and ports, and people capable of running them.

Trains from Silesia bring coal and iron to Berlin, along with new petitions. Railway companies seek support for freight services, while manufacturers want to expand the production of machinery and tools. The officers favour more transport capacity, though they have drawn up their own calculations for its use. The government must decide where further support will go.
Our workshops need their own machinery.

Provincial schools are training a new generation of teachers and officials. Some want them to serve their own communities; others would bring them into Vienna's administration. Both claim to be strengthening the country. Their disagreement concerns where education and authority should take root.

Shipping records and tax accounts are beginning to show the results of recent investment. Merchants ask that support remain with the ports, while treasury officials see an opportunity to strengthen administration. The government cannot rely indefinitely on extraordinary levies. Further investment calls for a choice.
Support the ports and their commerce.
Put administration on a lasting footing.

Egyptian workshops can now turn more of the country's cotton into cloth. Manufacturers seek help to expand. Teachers warn the government that an industry cannot prosper for long if literacy and technical knowledge remain the preserve of a few. The first gains of prosperity have brought another decision.
Schools must keep pace with industry.

Schools, ports and workshops have given the government achievements more substantial than declarations. Provincial representatives want continued support for local works; the government in the capital wants to consolidate its authority. New construction can spread without necessarily bringing political credit to those who sponsored it.
Make this a foundation for public confidence.

Schools and transport in the South are beginning to show new life. Freed people seek wider access to education, while business interests press for continued railway support. Emancipation was a beginning. Further investment will shape the place of the newly free in the economy that follows.

Railways have linked some mining districts to the coast, and Lima's merchants are discussing larger investments. Mine owners want to expand production. Engineers fear that a shortage of skilled people will leave new machinery idle. The government can support further output or invest in the knowledge needed to sustain it.
Train people to master these techniques.
Circumstances no longer permit this arrangement.

The promised programme of improvements has not been completed. Schools, industry and transport remain pressing concerns, but the expectations surrounding this undertaking have faded. What has been built will remain in use. What was promised will not be so easily forgotten.
